item.title: ChatGPT Wallet: network tokens, one biometric approval per purchase and no OpenAI fee at launch. What merchants and security teams should do now
item.description: OpenAI's dots agents can now check out with Visa, Mastercard and American Express without ever seeing a card number; the design sets a bar other agent payments will be judged against, and the economics are deliberately unstated.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI's dots agents can now check out with Visa, Mastercard and American Express without ever seeing a card number; the design sets a bar other agent payments will be judged against, and the economics are deliberately unstated.

OpenAI switched on ChatGPT Wallet on Thursday for a limited number of US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and over. The feature gives dots, the always-on personal agents OpenAI introduced on September 29, a way to pay. The design choices are more interesting than the launch itself, because they are the choices every other agent-payments product will now be compared with.

How a purchase works

The user adds an eligible US-issued Visa, Mastercard or American Express card once. A dot browses to a merchant's existing checkout, assembles the basket, and ChatGPT shows a review screen listing the items, the total and the card. The user approves with Face ID or a fingerprint. Only then does the card network issue a payment token, a limited-use number with its own security code and expiry, which the agent enters at checkout. The merchant receives valid card details that are not the real card; the agent never sees either. Rewards and dispute rights stay with the underlying card, and disputes go through the issuer as usual. Each approval creates a record of what the agent was authorised to buy, which is the piece auditors will care about.

What does not exist yet: spending limits, category limits, time windows or pre-approved purchases. OpenAI says those are planned without dates. Every purchase today needs a human tap, so a dot cannot buy anything on its own. Purchases also fail where sites block agents or fraud systems flag agent traffic, which OpenAI acknowledges.

The merchant side

Merchants need no Wallet-specific integration; existing checkout pages work. OpenAI's Commerce Partner Playbook nonetheless gives retailers a list: allow verified ChatGPT browser visits through CDNs and firewalls, submit product feeds, read the Forwarded HTTP header for the user's country, locale, time zone and device, offer a plugin with structured actions, add Sign in with ChatGPT, and maintain a Business Profile. Fraud vendors Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and processors Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe are named partners. Tokens cannot be stored or reused by the merchant; recurring billing needs explicit consent and processor support.

The context is the week United Airlines amended its contract of carriage to ban agents from booking, supervised or not. OpenAI's answer is a verified, tokenised, human-approved flow that gives merchants a reason to say yes. Whether they do will depend on chargeback rates nobody has yet published.

The economics OpenAI is not stating

OpenAI told CNBC it is not collecting a share of transaction revenue at launch. The phrase is precise. Meta's Muse already pays through Link by Stripe; PayPal has its own deal to sit inside ChatGPT as a payments wallet; the earlier Instant Checkout programme came with a merchant fee. A purchase graph across a user base OpenAI puts at 1.2 billion weekly is worth more as leverage over merchants than as a 2% take, at least until the merchants are locked in. The playbook's ranking signals, product feeds and Business Profiles, are where that leverage will be exercised first.

What to do

Retailers: decide this month whether verified ChatGPT agent traffic is allowed, and if so, instrument it separately so you can see conversion and chargebacks before the volume arrives. Security teams: adopt the pattern, network tokens, per-transaction human approval and a signed authorisation record, as the minimum for any internal purchasing agent, and ask your card issuer whether it offers tokens to your own automation. Finance: watch for the first announcement of spending limits and pre-approved purchases, because autonomous buying is when the fee conversation starts. Everyone: read the Forwarded-header guidance; it tells you exactly what an agent discloses about its user, and that list will become a privacy question.

item.title: United Airlines wrote AI agents into its contract of carriage as a prohibited practice: what the text says and what retailers should take from it
item.description: Supervision is no defence, searching is still allowed and United can cancel without notice; the first airline ban on agents is a template other merchants will copy or reject.
item.content:encoded:
Supervision is no defence, searching is still allowed and United can cancel without notice; the first airline ban on agents is a template other merchants will copy or reject.

United Airlines revised its contract of carriage on November 11 to prohibit AI agents from making, modifying or servicing tickets or buying any product, and to let it cancel reservations made that way without notice. It is the first major US carrier to put the rule in the contract passengers accept when they buy a ticket; Delta was reported in October to be blocking similar tools technically. The Wall Street Journal first reported the change.

What the text says

A new definition in Rule 1 describes an AI agent as software or services, including AI assistants, agents or AI-enabled browsers, that take autonomous or semi-autonomous action to discover, search, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage United products on behalf of a passenger or anyone else, whether or not a person supervises or approves what the software does. The examples cover assistants built into social, messaging and search platforms, AI browsers and standalone agents, and third-party assistants reaching United through a travel agency's tools. Rule 6.J.6 adds the use of such agents to the list of prohibited ticketing practices, alongside hidden-city and throwaway ticketing. Rule 5.H adds reservations made, modified or serviced by agents to the bookings United may cancel without notifying anyone. Existing remedies for prohibited practices include voiding tickets, charging the full fare after travel, deleting miles, revoking status and terminating MileagePlus membership. Bookings made before November 11 are not affected, assistive technology for passengers with disabilities is exempt, and travel agencies may use AI tools only with United's permission.

What is still allowed

The definition covers discovering and searching, but the prohibition covers only making, modifying or servicing a ticket and purchasing. Using an assistant to find and compare fares and then buying on united.com yourself is permitted, which is also the model Expedia's ChatGPT integration already follows: show the options, send the customer to checkout. United has not defined 'service a ticket', has not said how it will detect agents, and says agent bookings are rare today and that it works with no third-party agents.

United's reasons, and the other one

United cites three: passengers sharing logins with third-party tools expose personal data; agents can make unintended purchases, account changes or spend miles; and federal dangerous-goods rules require a passenger to personally acknowledge warnings at purchase and check-in, which an automated check-in would bypass. Chief executive Scott Kirby reportedly gave a fourth at an event in Chicago: he did not want to create another middleman. Analyst Henry Harteveldt told CBS that searches cost airlines money and agents generate searches that do not convert, which is the same economics that pushed Amazon to cut off Meta's Muse agent in September and win an injunction against Perplexity's Comet in March. Walmart went the other way in October, publishing terms and spending limits under which outside agents may transact.

The counter-argument

A contractual ban is not a technical one. A booking record may show Expedia as the seller and nothing about the assistant that drove it, and United's own definition catches a customer who approves every step, which is the behaviour the HUMAN Security survey in June found 54% of Americans comfortable with for planning and 12% for autonomous booking. Punishing the customer's loyalty account for a tool choice is the part most likely to be tested, in court or by the Department of Transportation, which has already asked United, Delta and JetBlue to explain how they set fares. And the last industry attempt to police booking channels, American's move to deny miles on some agency bookings, was walked back.

What to do

If you build agents: implement a merchant policy check, stop at fare display on united.com, and log the hand-off so you can show a customer did the buying. If you run a transactional site: write down which of the three postures you are taking, publish it in your terms, and instrument agent traffic now; Arkose reported in October that 97.7% of legitimate agent sessions carried no verified identity, so detection is a product decision, not a configuration. If you are a traveller: use AI to search, buy yourself, and do not hand your MileagePlus login to a browser extension. Watch for Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and similar schemes, because a verified, paying agent is the version of this that airlines will eventually welcome.

item.title: OpenAI's $10 billion quarter came with a $10.9 billion loss: what the leaked numbers say next to Anthropic's S-1
item.description: Revenue up 50% in a quarter, enterprise now bigger than consumer, and a loss of $1.09 per dollar of sales; the figures explain the Cursor cutoff, the Astra price and why OpenAI's IPO is a 2027 story.
item.content:encoded:
Revenue up 50% in a quarter, enterprise now bigger than consumer, and a loss of $1.09 per dollar of sales; the figures explain the Cursor cutoff, the Astra price and why OpenAI's IPO is a 2027 story.

OpenAI took in about $10 billion of revenue in the third quarter, up roughly 50% from $6.7 billion in the second, according to internal documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and reported on November 11. Its adjusted operating loss grew to about $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion. The company has not confirmed the figures, has not published net loss, compute spending or cash, and files no public accounts; Forbes and others carried the numbers with the Journal's attribution, and so do we.

The numbers in one table

Revenue of $10 billion against an adjusted operating loss of $10.9 billion is a margin of minus 109%, better than the minus 150% of the previous quarter. Put another way, OpenAI lost $1.09 for every dollar it sold, down from $1.50. Chief financial officer Sarah Friar reportedly told staff that enterprise revenue doubled quarter on quarter, driven largely by coding tools, while consumer subscriptions grew 20%. That makes enterprise the largest revenue line for the first time, a shift that happened faster than OpenAI's own September guidance of a near-$70 billion run rate implied.

The Anthropic comparison, with its caveats

Anthropic's amended S-1, filed for an IPO that prices on November 18, shows $16.96 billion of revenue in the same quarter, up 47%, with an operating loss of $567 million and a net loss of $23.3 billion that is mostly a non-cash charge on convertible notes. On revenue, OpenAI is about 59% the size of Anthropic. On operating loss, OpenAI's is about nineteen times larger. The bases differ: Anthropic's are audited figures in a securities filing, OpenAI's are adjusted internal numbers, and 'adjusted' at a private company can exclude stock compensation, some compute commitments or both. The direction is still unambiguous. Two companies with similar products have chosen opposite points on the growth-versus-margin curve, and only one of them has to explain that choice to public investors next week.

Why the loss is a strategy

OpenAI's losses are not an accident of scale; they are the price of owning distribution. ChatGPT reaches 1.2 billion people a week, most of them free. The Businesses in ChatGPT launch this week, with claimable profiles and sponsored agents, is the start of monetising that audience with advertising rather than subscriptions. The enterprise doubling shows the other leg: coding tools and platform commitments, including the ChatGPT Enterprise listing on AWS Marketplace that lets buyers draw down cloud commitments. Cutting Cursor off today, in the quarter coding drove revenue, only makes sense if OpenAI believes its own coding products capture that spend. GPT-6 Astra at $10 per million input tokens and $50 output is priced to recover margin on the customers who cannot leave.

The counter-argument

The bull case is simple: revenue grew 50% in a quarter and losses grew 8%. Extend both lines and the margin problem solves itself within a year. The bear case is that the loss is adjusted, compute commitments with Oracle, Microsoft and the chip vendors run to hundreds of billions over five years, and the quarter's growth came from the one segment, coding, where Anthropic, Google and now SpaceX's Cursor are competing hardest on price. Friar said in August that OpenAI 'will be a public company in 2027' and the company filed confidentially in June. Anthropic's pricing next week sets the comparable; a $1.4 trillion valuation on $17 billion of quarterly revenue would be a gift to OpenAI's bankers, and a stumble would not be.

What to watch

Anthropic's IPO pricing on November 18 and first trades on November 19; whether OpenAI leaks a fourth-quarter revenue figure or run rate before year end; the first ad-revenue disclosure from Businesses in ChatGPT; and the December 31 end of the GPT-6 Astra for Law promotional price, the next scheduled signal on whether OpenAI is prepared to raise prices on captive segments. For buyers, the practical conclusion is that OpenAI needs your renewal more than you need its roadmap this quarter, which is the moment to negotiate.

item.title: Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Meetings: Anthropic now sells an office suite, and here is what IT buyers should ask before the renewal
item.description: The day before its roadshow, Anthropic turned Claude from a chat window into a workspace with spreadsheets, shared boards, embedded partner apps and a meeting participant; the licence conversation changes with it.
item.content:encoded:
The day before its roadshow, Anthropic turned Claude from a chat window into a workspace with spreadsheets, shared boards, embedded partner apps and a meeting participant; the licence conversation changes with it.

Anthropic released a set of workplace products on November 10 that moves Claude out of the chat box. Claude Sheets lets a team and Claude build spreadsheets together across tabs, with formulas, formatting and dropdowns, and with every change Claude makes written to a log. Claude Whiteboards is a shared board for planning sessions that Claude can turn into timelines and then export as a document or slide deck. Claude Data, the product formerly called Dashboards, is generally available and connects to warehouses and CRMs such as Snowflake and Salesforce; certified data definitions from a customer's data team are in beta. And partners including Adobe and Atlassian can now embed full versions of their applications inside Claude over MCP, with Salesforce, NetSuite and Workday plugins shipping with built-in skills.

TechCrunch reported a fifth product, Claude Meetings, in beta on Team and Enterprise plans: Claude joins a Google Meet call as a visible participant, drafts plans and whiteboards while people are still talking, pulls material from connected apps and leaves notes and action items in claude.ai afterwards. It announces itself in the meeting chat, will not join calls with external guests unless an admin allows it, and leaves if an outside guest arrives. Anthropic's own article lists Meetings as "coming soon", so treat the beta as limited.

Why the timing matters

The launch came one day before Anthropic opened its IPO roadshow at a range that values it at up to $1.4 trillion. A product line that competes with Excel, Miro, Tableau and the note-taking half of Teams supports a revenue story that is not only API tokens, and investors read it that way: Microsoft fell 2.2% to $533.16 on the day and briefly lost its newly regained second place among listed companies. OpenAI shipped its own data-visualisation and presentation tools in September, and Meta's Muse agent builds throwaway mini-apps. The three largest labs are now converging on the same claim, that the AI assistant should be the surface where work happens rather than a tab beside it.

What changes for buyers

Most Claude enterprise contracts were written as model access plus a chat seat. The new products pull in three things that were previously someone else's procurement problem. The first is data. Claude Data with certified definitions means your semantic layer lives partly in Anthropic's product, and Sheets means formulas and business logic do too. The second is partner apps. An Adobe or Atlassian session running inside Claude runs under that vendor's licence and data terms as well as Anthropic's, and the admin controls Anthropic describes, per-connector permissions such as read Slack but do not post, granular spend limits and audit logs through a Compliance API that talks to Splunk and CrowdStrike, are the controls you will need to map to each. The third is presence. A meeting participant that drafts documents from a live conversation is a recording device for the purposes of most jurisdictions' consent rules and most companies' legal-hold policies.

Anthropic's Enterprise architecture, as described in its article, runs each cloud session in an isolated virtual machine and keeps connector credentials outside it, with data encrypted in transit and at rest. The article does not say which tiers get Sheets, Whiteboards or Data, and gives no prices; Meetings is Team and Enterprise only per TechCrunch.

The counter-argument

Microsoft and Google have the files, the identity system and the calendar. A spreadsheet that lives in Claude is useful until a controller needs it in Excel with the audit trail intact, and an exported whiteboard is a copy, not a system of record. The history of productivity suites is that distribution beats features, and the two incumbents have both bundled their own assistants at near-zero marginal price. Anthropic's bet is that the agent, not the file format, becomes the system of record; that bet is not yet proven anywhere.

What to ask

Before renewing, ask which products are in your tier and at what seat price; whether the isolated-VM architecture applies to your plan; how Sheets and Data content is retained, exported and deleted at contract end; whether Meetings transcripts fall under your retention and discovery policies and who holds them; which partner terms apply when Adobe or Atlassian run inside Claude; and whether the change log in Sheets is exportable for audit. Pilot Sheets with one finance team on non-controlled data and compare the formula quality against a Copilot or Gemini workbook. Then decide whether Claude is a platform in your architecture diagram or an application in someone else's.

item.title: Google's four TPUs in one year: what 8tx and 8i Max mean for anyone negotiating with Nvidia
item.description: Confidential compute for fine-tuning and a doubled-up inference chip extend the eighth-generation line, and the software around it is now the real competitive move.
item.content:encoded:
Confidential compute for fine-tuning and a doubled-up inference chip extend the eighth-generation line, and the software around it is now the real competitive move.

Google announced two more eighth-generation TPU systems on November 9, bringing to four the number it has introduced this year, a cadence it says it has never managed before. TPU 8t for large-scale training and TPU 8i for real-time inference arrived at Cloud Next in April; TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max complete the set.

The two new systems

TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as 8t but pairs it with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host CPUs to deliver hardware-level confidential computing, keeping both data and model weights isolated while in use. Google positions it for secure inference and for small-scale training, fine-tuning, distillation and reinforcement learning on sensitive data that cannot leave a customer's trust boundary. It borrows the Boardfly interconnect from 8i and Google claims up to half the latency of 8t with a negligible performance penalty.

TPU 8i Max packages two 8i chips together, doubling compute, on-chip SRAM and HBM bandwidth per package while fitting into the existing rack footprint. It is aimed at very long context windows and at squeezing more compute out of each square foot and each watt, the two constraints that now bind data-centre operators more than chip supply does. Google gave no pricing or availability dates for either system.

The software is the story

The hardware announcements came wrapped in a software release that matters more for adoption. TorchTPU, open-sourced in October, lets PyTorch code and Hugging Face models run natively on TPUs, with backends for the vLLM and SGLang serving engines that most inference teams already use. An open-source XLA Serving Engine runs models across TPUs, GPUs and CPUs from one C++ runtime. TPU Sync tiers key-value caches across chip memory, host DRAM and storage, and Google claims it cuts cache transfer latency and time-to-first-token by more than 90%. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing, which assemble and partition TPU topologies through optical circuit switching, are now generally available. There is even a preview TPU agent suite that plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Antigravity to diagnose bottlenecks and autotune kernels.

For years the honest objection to TPUs was that the software assumed JAX and a Google-shaped workflow. That objection is now largely gone, which is why the claim of nearly 100 TPU customers, including frontier labs and trading firms, is more credible than it would have been in 2024.

Why Nvidia buyers should care

Nvidia's pricing power rests on CUDA lock-in and on the absence of a second supplier that can deliver training-class systems at scale. Four TPU systems in a year, with a PyTorch-native stack and confidential compute, is the most direct challenge to both. Buyers rarely need to move workloads to benefit: a credible alternative in the room changes the terms of a GPU reservation or a multi-year cloud commitment. It also arrives in a week when Nvidia's own governance is under an independent board review, which sharpens any procurement committee's interest in a second source.

The counter-argument

TPUs are only available through Google Cloud, so the choice is also a choice of cloud, and that lock-in is arguably tighter than CUDA's. Google's performance claims are its own and the two new systems have no public pricing. Most enterprise inference still runs on models whose vendors optimise first for Nvidia, and Anthropic's new Fable 5.2 fast mode, for example, is available on Google Cloud but was engineered on mixed hardware. The practical gap between 'runs on TPU' and 'runs best on TPU' is where migration projects stall.

What to do

Ask your Google account team for 8tx and 8i Max pricing and dates in writing. Run one production inference service through vLLM on TPU 8i and compare cost per million output tokens against your current GPU fleet. If you handle regulated data, request the confidential-compute attestation flow for 8tx and have your security team review it. And whatever the outcome, bring the numbers to your next Nvidia or cloud renewal.

item.title: Nvidia's board is investigating Jensen Huang. Here is what is actually at stake
item.description: An independent review, an admitted affair and a November 18 congressional briefing turn a personal scandal into a governance test for the company the whole AI stack depends on.
item.content:encoded:
An independent review, an admitted affair and a November 18 congressional briefing turn a personal scandal into a governance test for the company the whole AI stack depends on.

Nvidia's board of directors announced on Sunday, November 8, that its independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, will review CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. The same day, Huang sent a message to employees acknowledging an affair with her, apologising to his family and colleagues and saying he had fallen short of his responsibility to the company.

The board's statement paired the review with two reassurances: it said it has "no reason to believe" national-security or company secrets were compromised, and that it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Huang said he supports the review and will cooperate.

How we got here

We covered the first chapter yesterday: a New York Times report that a memo circulated among US policymakers earlier this year alleged Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Nvidia's chief executive. Nvidia's initial response was that the two executives' interactions were "not unusual" and that the company does not share classified information with customers. Megaspeed is a Nvidia customer, and the company has been a focus of earlier reporting on how advanced GPUs reach China despite US export controls.

What changed on Sunday is that the personal relationship is no longer in dispute, and the board has formally taken ownership of the question. House committee chairs had already requested a closed-door briefing from Huang, scheduled for November 18.

Why this is a governance story, not a gossip story

Nvidia is not a normal company. Its GPUs run the overwhelming majority of frontier AI training, its export licences are a lever of US foreign policy, and its chief executive is the single most influential individual in the AI supply chain. A founder-CEO in that position who was, on the available reporting, in a relationship with a suspected intelligence asset raises three distinct questions a board has to answer separately.

First, was anything disclosed that should not have been? The board says it has no reason to think so, but that is a starting position, not a finding. Second, did the relationship create leverage, regardless of whether anything was disclosed? Counter-intelligence professionals treat a secret affair as a classic coercion vector, which is why executive-protection programmes at defence contractors cover personal conduct. Third, does the episode change how Washington treats Nvidia's China business, which is already under scrutiny from both parties?

Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, who studies CEO succession, told TechCrunch he puts Huang's survival odds at roughly 50-50. That is a sharper read than the board's language, but it reflects a real pattern: boards that open independent reviews while expressing confidence usually mean it, and the outcome tends to turn on what the review finds rather than on the initial scandal.

The counter-argument

The case for calm is that Nvidia's commercial position does not depend on one person. Its software moat, supply agreements and customer relationships are institutional. A leadership transition at a $4-trillion-class company would be disruptive but survivable, and the stock has absorbed worse news in the past week, when the Nasdaq 100 shed a record $2.3 trillion and Nvidia alone lost around $450 billion in value on election and demand worries.

The case against calm is that Huang is unusually central to Nvidia's strategy, its China diplomacy and its customer relationships, and that this story has moved from a single-outlet report to a board action and an admission in nine days.

What to watch

The November 18 congressional briefing is the next hard date. Watch whether any part of it becomes public, whether the Commerce Department or BIS reference the episode in any export-licensing decision, and whether the board sets a timetable for the review. Also watch Megaspeed: any regulatory action against it would reopen the chip-diversion thread this story grew out of. We will update this article as the review progresses.

item.title: Ramp's data says business AI spending has flattened. Here is how to read it
item.description: A plateau in the share of companies paying for AI tools is not the end of adoption. It is the end of buying everything.
item.content:encoded:
A plateau in the share of companies paying for AI tools is not the end of adoption. It is the end of buying everything.

Ramp, the corporate card and bill-pay company, publishes an index built from what its customers actually pay for. TechCrunch reported on November 6 that the latest reading shows the share of US businesses paying for AI tools has flattened in recent months after two years of steady growth. The timing, days before Anthropic's IPO marketing begins, guaranteed attention.

What the data measures, and what it does not

Ramp's index measures breadth: the fraction of businesses with at least one AI subscription or usage charge. It is a good proxy for "has tried AI," and that number saturating was always going to happen; most companies that were going to buy a ChatGPT or Claude seat have done so.

It does not measure depth: how much each adopter spends, how many seats, how much API usage. Breadth can flatten while depth rises, which is the pattern in most enterprise software categories after the trial phase. It also undercounts spend that flows through cloud bills (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud), where most API usage is invoiced.

The pilot cull

What is almost certainly happening underneath is consolidation. Two years of experimentation produced, in many companies, five or six overlapping subscriptions and several pilots with no owner. Finance teams are now cancelling what did not produce measurable results and standardising on one or two platforms. That shows up as flat breadth and, often, higher spend per surviving vendor.

Why it matters for the IPO

Investors underwriting Anthropic, and OpenAI's next round, are paying for growth that depends on enterprise expansion. Flat adoption breadth is not fatal to that story, but it moves the burden of proof to depth: usage per customer, net revenue retention and API growth, numbers the S-1 and the roadshow will be pushed to disclose.

What to do with it

  • If you run a company: make the consolidation deliberate. List every AI line item, assign an owner and an outcome, and cancel the rest. The survivors will get better terms if you consolidate volume.
  • If you sell AI software: the land-grab phase is over. Expansion now comes from proving outcomes inside existing accounts, not from logos.
  • If you invest: ask every AI company for net revenue retention. It is the number this data makes unavoidable.
